project.name: Not Arbitrary 09 — The Horse Is Standing on Its Tail

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: The Chinese character for horse is a drawing of a horse. It is hard to see because the first people to write it stood the horse on its tail.
entries.direction: Warm, unhurried, a little amused. State the first sentence plainly, then a small pause before the second, and let 'on its tail' land lightly.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Draw a horse the way anyone would. Side on, facing left, with a mane down the back of its neck, four legs, and a tail.
entries.direction: Plain and physical, as if drawing along with the listener. Unhurried through the list of parts.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Three thousand years ago, scribes carving into ox bones and turtle shells drew this same animal, and they drew it standing up.
entries.direction: A little lift of wonder on 'three thousand years ago'. Land 'standing up' simply, no emphasis.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Over the centuries that followed, the legs came back down underneath it. But the neck stayed upright, and the mane still streams out sideways, the way it would on a horse standing on its tail.
entries.direction: Measured. A clear turn on 'But'. The second sentence is the argument of the shot, so keep it as one unhurried phrase.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: That is the character for horse, and it is still written this way today. The three lines are its mane, and the four dots along the bottom are its legs.
entries.direction: The reveal. Simple and warm, let it sit. A small smile on 'its legs'.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: It was never only the horse. The tiger, the dog, the pig and the elephant were all written standing on their tails.
entries.direction: A new thread, so lift slightly at the start. Give each animal its own small beat.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Lay them back down, and every one of them is plainly an animal. A rule kept that consistently has a reason behind it.
entries.direction: Gentle, almost pleased. Then slightly more deliberate on the second sentence, setting up the turn.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: The reason is the page. Books in ancient China were strips of bamboo, each about as wide as a finger, tied side by side with cord.
entries.direction: The turn of the film. Slow down. A definite pause after 'The reason is the page', then concrete and physical.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: A horse lying down is wider than a finger. So the scribe turned the horse instead.
entries.direction: Dry and matter of fact. A beat before 'So'. Land 'instead' quietly.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: The strips left a second mark. For three thousand years, Chinese was written in columns, from the top down, because a strip of bamboo only has room for one.
entries.direction: Unhurried, a small lift on 'a second mark'. Keep 'from the top down' clear.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Not one bamboo book survives from that age. Bamboo rots, and bone does not. We only know those books existed because the writing has a word for one.
entries.direction: Quiet and precise, like laying out evidence. A small pause after 'bone does not'.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Strips of different lengths, and the cord that bound them together. That character is still in use, long after anyone stopped writing on bamboo.
entries.direction: The second reveal. Warm and simple, a little wondering on the last clause.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: A horse, and a book made of bamboo. The shape of the page decided the shape of the writing, and the writing kept that shape long after the page was gone.
entries.direction: Gather it up. Warm, a little wondering, not a summary read.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: You are still reading the shape of a page that nobody alive has ever seen.
entries.direction: Land it and stop. No lift at the end.
